# About this edition

The first edition collected practices for building an ontology with an LLM and
keeping it useful to people and systems. This edition keeps its four parts
(authoring, sharing, data, lifecycle) and revises them after one proof of
concept that followed the guide end to end: an ontology, its validation loop,
a generated SQLite database, a data dictionary and a business glossary, built
with Claude Code and then changed once after its first release. The examples
come from that project instead of finance and controlling.

The main changes, each explained where it belongs:

- a new **first step**: state how the key concepts relate, in a few sentences a
  domain expert can judge, before writing competency questions;
- competency questions with **expected answers written by the expert by hand**,
  tested in **two query layers** (SPARQL and SQL);
- **reuse by definition, not by name**, checked against the vocabulary's own file;
- every check in the validation loop has a **negative test**, and every
  generated artifact a **drift check**;
- the source's **packaging is not the domain**: file splits, pagination and API
  resources must not become concepts;
- **physical design** as part of the bridge from shapes to schema;
- **iterating on a released model**: the steps to revisit, and deprecation in
  every generated artifact.

## The worked example

The Police of the Czech Republic publish offence records as open data
(*Mapa kriminality*, `kriminalita.policie.gov.cz`). Each record is one act
reported to or detected by the police, with a report date and time, one or
more offence types from a three-level classification, a clearance state
(probable offender identified, unsolved, act did not occur, not an offence),
what the published place stands for (place of commission, of report, …), and
an anonymised place. The data are downloaded as monthly CSV files, which are
regenerated as investigations progress.

The proof of concept built a continuous history of one year: 1.38 million
records, one row per occurrence in its latest state, each record placed in one
of 39,927 anonymisation areas and each area in one of 6,258 municipalities.
The data are small enough to reason about and real enough to contain every
difficulty this guide discusses.

# Part I: Authoring

## The recommended sequence

> Reconnaissance $\rightarrow$ concepts and how they relate $\rightarrow$
> competency questions $\rightarrow$ reuse survey $\rightarrow$ skeleton
> $\rightarrow$ definitions $\rightarrow$ reference data $\rightarrow$ shapes
> $\rightarrow$ test suite $\rightarrow$ validation loop $\rightarrow$ data model,
> loader, dictionary and glossary $\rightarrow$ iterate.

Each step says who does the work. In the proof of concept the split was
stable: the **LLM** drafts (questions, terms, definitions, shapes, queries),
the **human domain expert** decides (verdicts, hand answers, decisions in the
spec, wording in their language), and **scripts** do everything that must be
repeatable (reference data, schema, dictionary, glossary, validation, loading).
None of it needs a GUI editor; the source files plus the validation loop are
the ontology.

**Reconnaissance, with a warning.** When the ontology describes an existing
dataset, read the source first: its documentation, codelists and a sample of
records. But the source's packaging is not the domain. In the example, the
publisher splits downloads by month to keep files manageable; the first draft
modelled a *monthly extract* as a concept, and four competency questions
grouped by it. The domain expert caught it, not a tool. Ask the expert, for
each structure in the source: does this carry meaning, or is it delivery?

## Practice 1: State how the concepts relate, before anything else

Before the competency questions, write the relationships between the key
concepts as **a handful of sentences in domain language**, each with both
ends: *how many of B for one A, and how many of A for one B*. The domain expert
marks each one true, false or "depends". A judgement takes seconds and needs
no technical knowledge.

> *An offence record has one or more offence types; an offence type covers any
> number of records.*
>
> *An offence record is placed in exactly one anonymisation area; an area holds
> any number of records.*
>
> *An anonymisation area lies in exactly one municipality; a municipality has
> one or more areas.*

Ask two questions of each sentence: is it true **in the world**, and is it what
**the source** chose to keep? An offence can involve several places (where it
was reported, committed, or had consequences); the publisher keeps one per
record and says which kind it is. Writing both answers down keeps the source's
choices from passing as facts of the domain.

Why this step: the two largest corrections in the example were structural, not
wrong answers. The monthly extract was modelled as a concept, and the
anonymised place as a value on the record when it is a shared area (many
records, one area). Competency questions caught neither, because they ask for
answers, not for what exists and how many.

Keep it short, or it stops being the expert's. The LLM's first draft had 21
statements; most were about attributes (identifier, dates, flags), which no
domain expert has an opinion on and which belong to the shapes. Cut to
relationships only, both ends in one sentence, the current model only, it was
seven. An LLM drafting a checklist tends to make it complete rather than short;
ask what the checklist is *for*.

Make the sentences traceable: each names the SHACL shape that enforces it, and
the validation loop checks that every sentence marked true is enforced with
the same cardinality, and that no shape enforces a sentence marked false. A true
sentence not yet modelled is a warning: a to-do for the later steps.

## Practice 2: Competency questions are an executable spec

Have the LLM draft 15–30 questions the ontology must answer, with precise
parameters and the **decision** each one forces, and treat the file as the
specification. In the example:

> *CQ03. For each category, how many records are there, how many have a
> probable offender identified, and what is the clearance rate?*
> *Decision: records concluded as "act did not occur" or "not an offence" are
> excluded from the denominator; categories with no remaining records are
> omitted.*

Then make the questions executable, in four ways the first edition did not
spell out:

- **The expert writes the expected answers by hand**, from a small sample, for
  the key questions. The value is in the disagreements. In the example, five
  hand answers took ten disagreements to settle: three slips by the expert,
  five imprecise questions or data presentations, two faults of the validator.
  A method that treats the expert as the oracle would have "fixed" the queries
  to match a slip; one that treats the queries as the oracle would have missed
  the imprecise questions. In the second iteration, with sharper questions,
  both hand answers matched on the first try.
- **Never show the expert the computed answer** before they commit to theirs.
  On failure, the validator says *where* an answer disagrees (missing rows,
  which columns differ) but not the values, unless asked.
- **Answer every question in two query layers** where a database is the
  target: SPARQL on the sample RDF and SQL on a database generated from the
  same sample, and require them to agree. In the example this caught a silent
  tooling failure: a SPARQL engine that mishandled escaped prefixed names
  returned zero burglaries without an error.
- **Give the sample in the format of the reader's task.** For answering by
  hand, that is CSV for a spreadsheet, with helper columns (a record's
  categories, each area's municipality), not a Markdown table. Questions that
  depend on empty groups should say whether empty groups are listed (records
  per area: list empty areas as 0) or omitted (records per municipality: omit
  municipalities with no records), because the expert will ask.

A question the data cannot answer is recorded as a **known gap** with what
closing it would take. In the example, *which municipality?* was a gap in the
first version and was closed in the second.

## Practice 3: Pick an LLM-friendly source format

Turtle for OWL and SHACL remains a good choice: compact, readable in diffs,
close to what the model has seen. The example used Turtle for the ontology and
the shapes, CSV for hand-maintained translations of codelist items, and
Markdown for the two specification files (concept sentences and competency
questions), with fenced blocks the validator parses. LinkML is the alternative
when the ontology is mostly a data model; the example did not need it, because
about 300 lines of Python (an interpreter of the shapes and a DDL generator) turned the shapes into SQL (Part III).

## Practice 4: Write for natural-language readers

An LLM reads an ontology through its text. Every class and property gets a
label, a definition in genus–differentia form, an example, and a scope note
saying what it does not cover:

> *An offence record is an information record, kept by the Police of the Czech
> Republic, about one act reported to or detected by the police that is
> suspected to be a crime or a misdemeanour.*
> *Scope note: the record, not the act; a record exists even when the police
> later conclude that the act did not occur.*

**Two definitions, two audiences.** Keep the formal definition in English for
modellers, and give business readers a second, plain definition in their own
language (`krim:businessDefinition@cs` in the example), not a translation of
the first. Use the publisher's own terms where they exist (*třída deliktu*,
the publisher's word, not a translation of "offence type"). Have a native
speaker review the business text; an LLM's translations are usable but
awkward.

**Every rule as a sentence.** Each SHACL property shape carries the rule as one
plain sentence, in both languages: *"Every offence record lies in exactly one
anonymisation area."* The glossary and the dictionary print these sentences;
the validator checks that each rule has one.

## Practice 5: Reuse by definition, not by name

Ask the LLM to propose existing vocabularies before inventing terms, and to
**read each candidate's own published file** before proposing a term from it,
instead of answering from memory. The example reused SKOS (codelists),
Dublin Core, PROV-O (a record is a `prov:Entity`; "state as of" refines
`prov:generatedAtTime`), WGS84 (coordinates), GeoSPARQL (areas and
municipalities are features; "lies in" refines `sfWithin`) and the term-status
vocabulary.

Three rules came out of it:

- **The definition decides, not the name.** GeoSPARQL's `hasCentroid` looked
  made for an area's centre. Its definition is the arithmetic mean of the
  geometry's points; the publisher's centre is a K-means cluster centre,
  sometimes moved inside the municipality. Reusing it would have asserted
  something false, quietly. The definition of the local term now says what the
  centre is *not*.
- **Link, don't adopt, fragile identifiers.** The publisher's codelist IRIs do
  not resolve and contain a typo and a version segment; they are linked with
  `skos:exactMatch`, not used as identifiers. A national register whose
  linked-data IRIs redirect to a web page is not linked at all; its code is the
  join key.
- **Exact or close, as the domain says.** The statistical office's codelist of
  municipalities includes four military training areas, which are not
  municipalities in law. The expert decided they count as municipalities in the
  project, so the class is a *close* match to the legal term, not an exact one.

Reused generic properties need a local name and definition when they become
data (Part III), and reused terms need OWL declarations so a DL reasoner
accepts them.

## Practice 6: Keep axioms modest and validate mechanically

A lean OWL model for meaning (no `rdfs:domain`/`rdfs:range`, a few
disjointness axioms) and SHACL for what valid data look like remains the right
split. The validation loop runs after every change, and in the example had
eight sections:

| Section | Passes when |
|---|---|
| Parse | all Turtle files parse |
| Reasoner | HermiT finds the model and sample consistent, *and* a contradictory individual inconsistent |
| Concepts | every concept sentence marked true is enforced by its shape, with the same cardinality |
| Lint | labels in both languages, one definition, a status, no duplicates, no undeclared terms, rules as sentences, dictionary and glossary text complete; a deprecated term names its replacement |
| SHACL | the sample conforms; exactly the expected warnings; each negative test fails for its stated reason |
| Generated artifacts | schema, dictionary, glossary, sample tables and the question index are current (drift check) |
| Competency questions | SPARQL = SQL = the expert's expected answer |
| Loader | one occurrence ends as one row in its latest state, in any load order; points are matched to areas |

: The validation loop {tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Three habits make the loop trustworthy:

- **Every check has a negative test.** A check that has never failed proves
  nothing. The example keeps invalid individuals, each breaking exactly one
  rule and annotated with the violation it must produce; a rule between two
  nodes (a duplicate identifier) also names the partner it flags.
- **Every generated artifact has a drift check.** The loop regenerates the
  schema, dictionary and glossary in memory and fails if the committed files
  differ. Generated files are never edited by hand.
- **Don't bend the checker to fit an answer.** When the expert's answer failed
  for a missing separator, the right fix was the answer, not a more lenient
  parser. A crashed section is reported as a failure and the others still run.

The typical LLM errors of the first edition all appeared, plus new ones; they
are collected in Appendix A.

## Practice 7: Small modules under git, with a CLAUDE.md

One file per module, a `CLAUDE.md` with namespaces, naming and definition
style, the reused vocabularies, which files are generated and from what, and
the validation command. Work in a branch per iteration, merge with a merge
commit so an iteration stays one unit in the history, and tag each release.
A commit may knowingly fail validation in the middle of an iteration (in the
example, the shapes changed before the sample data did) if the commit message
names the expected failures and the next step clears them.

# Part II: Sharing with non-technical readers

The ontology stays the single source; everything business readers see is
generated from it. In the example the reader was a domain expert who reads
Czech: the raw data are Czech, so the business glossary is Czech, clearly
distinct from the English data dictionary. The principle is **English
internals, Czech business translations**.

## Choose the format by the reader's task

| Deliverable | Reader's task | Format |
|---|---|---|
| Business glossary | read, look up, print | PDF table (landscape), in the readers' language |
| Data dictionary | review and comment | Excel with *Comments* and *Agree?* columns; PDF and CSV for reference |
| Sample data | answer questions by hand | CSV for a spreadsheet |
| Specification (concept sentences, competency questions) | edit and decide | Markdown, in git |

: Formats by task {tbl-colwidths="[26,30,44]"}

The first edition proposed Excel for the glossary. In the example the reader
asked for a PDF: a glossary is read, not edited, and comments go to the
dictionary review.

## What the glossary contains

One row per current term: the term, its plain definition, an example, what it
is not to be confused with, other names, and where it is recorded in the data
dictionary. Deprecated terms are left out; the dictionary keeps them.

| Pojem | Význam | Příklad | Nezaměňovat s |
|---|---|---|---|
| **anonymizační oblast** | Oblast, do jejíhož středu vydavatel posune místo každého skutku, který v ní leží. | Oblast 29789 v Praze. | Správní jednotka nebo skutečné místo skutku. |
| **třída deliktu** | Třída kriminalisticko-statistické evidence Policie ČR, podle které se záznamy třídí podle druhu skutku. | Krádeže vloupáním – byt (kód 19). | Právní kvalifikace podle trestního zákoníku. |

: Glossary entries from the example (*anonymisation area*, *offence type*) {tbl-colwidths="[18,40,20,22]"}

Besides the terms, the glossary carries the record rules as sentences, a few
worked examples generated from the sample data (*"Record 1013 falls into two
categories, a crime type and a misdemeanour"*), the small codelists in full, the
type hierarchy as an indented tree, and a concept diagram drawn by Graphviz
from the shapes. Every page is stamped with the ontology release.

## Closing the loop

Send the Excel dictionary out for comments; the LLM reads the returned sheet,
proposes changes in the source, and shows the diff for approval. Corrections
to the Czech wording go into the source annotations (`@cs`), never into the
PDF. A disagreement between reviewers often reveals two concepts sharing one
name, which the ontology should resolve.

# Part III: Ontology and data

## Concepts, terms and data elements

Keep three layers apart:

| Layer | Lives in | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Concept | ontology (an IRI) | `krim:AnonymisationArea`: one of a fixed set of polygons to whose centre every recorded place inside it is moved |
| Term | glossary, per language | "anonymisation area", "anonymizační oblast", "Voroného polygon" |
| Data element | data dictionary, schema | `offence_record.area_id`: integer, references `anonymisation_area(id)` |

: Three layers {tbl-colwidths="[18,24,58]"}

The IRI is the join key between them. In ISO/IEC 11179 terms, a data element
is an object class (the class a table realises) plus a property (the property a
column realises) plus a value domain. The data dictionary in the example is
generated with 19 fields per column, from the ontology and the shapes, and is
also written into the database as a table.

**A reused generic property makes the dictionary vaguer.** A column that
realises `dcterms:identifier` inherits a definition that fits anything. Give
each such column a local name and definition on the shape (*"the publisher's
integer identifier of an offence record, stable across download files"*), or
use a specific sub-property. The validator enforces both.

## From shapes to schema, including physical design

SHACL maps almost one to one onto a relational schema. A small interpreter,
guided by a handful of database-mapping hints in a separate namespace
(`kdb:`), generated the whole SQLite schema:

| SHACL | SQL |
|---|---|
| node shape with `kdb:table` | table, with an IRI column |
| `sh:datatype`, `sh:minCount 1`, ranges | column type, NOT NULL, CHECK |
| `sh:maxCount 1` | a column; otherwise a link table |
| `sh:class C` | a foreign key to the table of C |
| language columns hint | one column per language |
| self-reference (`skos:broader`) | a recursive closure view |
| warning severity | not enforced; reported by the loader |
| foreign-key column | **an index** |
| `kdb:index`, `kdb:uniqueColumns` | an index; a unique index (the counterpart of a SPARQL uniqueness rule) |

: Shapes to SQL {tbl-colwidths="[40,60]"}

The last two rows are new in this edition. The generated schema was correct
but had no index on a new foreign key, and the first quality check on 1.38
million records ran for over ten minutes before it was stopped. SQLite does not
index foreign keys itself. A rule (index every foreign-key column) plus two
hints fixed it and kept the whole schema generated; a full rebuild takes under
two minutes. Asked whether to parallelise the load, the answer was no: the time
was in one query, not in a busy core. Measure before optimising.

## Ontology, reference data and operational data

| Content | Example | Lives in |
|---|---|---|
| Ontology | classes, properties, definitions, shapes | versioned Turtle files |
| Reference data: codelists | offence types, clearance states, location relevance; municipalities (ČSÚ codelist 43) | SKOS concept schemes generated next to the ontology |
| Reference data: datasets | 39,927 anonymisation areas | the database and the test sample only |
| Operational data | offence records | the database and the test sample only |

: Kinds of content {tbl-colwidths="[24,46,30]"}

The boundary between a codelist and a dataset is a new line in this edition. A
codelist is something people look up by code and agree on (6,258 municipalities
qualify); a list of 40,000 polygons is reference data, but nobody looks up an
area by its number, so it stays out of the Turtle files. Codelists are
generated from the publisher's files, with hand-maintained translations in one
CSV, and fill the lookup tables of the database, so the database and the
glossary share one source.

## Continuous history, not pagination

The example's goal was one row per occurrence in its latest known state. Each
record therefore has two times: the **report time** (when the act was
reported) and the **observation time** (when the publisher reported the state
we hold, `krim:stateAsOf`). The loader merges by "latest observation wins":
a record read again replaces the stored one if its observation is the same or
newer, whatever the order in which files are loaded. A clearance rate is then
an "as of" figure, and the dictionary says so.

The same separation applies to places: the publisher's point is not stored on
the record; it is matched to an area's centre (exactly, or within one
micro-degree, since the publisher rounds to six decimals). A point that is no
area's centre is reported and the record skipped, never placed in the nearest
area: a silent nearest-neighbour fix would hide that the publisher has changed
its areas.

Be polite to the source: cache downloads with the publisher's timestamp beside
them, fetch again only when the publisher has a newer version and the cached
copy is old enough, and offer an offline mode. A normal run costs one small
listing request.

## The test suite

Keep a small, hand-made sample next to the ontology: in the example, 13
fictional records with real codes and real areas, chosen so that every
competency question and every shape is exercised (a record that is both a
crime and a misdemeanour; areas with no records; a single-area military
training area), plus one clearly marked fictional area outside the country
that must raise the warning. Generate the spreadsheet versions from it; never
maintain them by hand.

# Part IV: Lifecycle

An ontology is released like a library other systems depend on. The rules of
the first edition held: identifiers are permanent, meanings do not change under
an IRI, terms are deprecated, never deleted, and every consumer records the
release it was built from (the schema carries a release table; the dictionary
and glossary are stamped).

## Iterating on a released model

The example's second iteration started from a domain fact found after release,
on the publisher's website rather than in the API documentation: every
published place is the centre of one of a fixed list of areas. The method
absorbed it as a loop, and every step had an obvious place for its part:

1. two new concept sentences (record in area, area in municipality), judged by
   the expert;
2. five new competency questions, one known gap closed;
3. a reuse survey, including what not to reuse (`hasCentroid`);
4. new terms, and the record's coordinates **deprecated**: `owl:deprecated
   true`, `dcterms:isReplacedBy` the area and its centre;
5. definitions in both languages; a new codelist from the statistical office;
6. new shapes, committed with the expected failures named;
7. new sample data, negative tests and queries;
8. a loader that matches places to areas; indexes by rule;
9. a release: version, prior version, regenerated artifacts, merge and tag.

**Deprecation reaches every artifact.** The deprecated term stays in the
ontology with its replacement; a lint rule requires the replacement and warns
while shapes still use the term; the data dictionary lists deprecated terms in
an appendix; the business glossary shows current terms only.

**A changed meaning is a breaking change.** Before 1.0, semantic versioning
marks it with a minor version: the example went from 0.1.0 to 0.2.0, with
`owl:priorVersion` pointing back. From 1.0 on, the same change would be a major
version.

**Renaming is free only before the first release.** In the example a property
was renamed (the timestamp turned out to be report time, not commission time)
and three terms were removed (the monthly extract) before 0.1.0; after a
release both would have required deprecation.

## Environments and releases

Keep the environment out of the IRIs; terms stay the same in development,
test and production, and only the version changes. Release the ontology,
shapes, schema, dictionary and glossary from the same commit, as one bundle.
Freeze releases when downstream consumers are busiest (a reporting close in
finance; a publisher's regeneration cycle here).

## Two time axes, again

Keep "which release defined this term" apart from "when was this item in
force". Reference data need effective dating inside the data (an area list
dated 2022 still matched every 2025 record; a municipality codelist has
validity dates per item), separately from the ontology's release number. The
data themselves add a third pair: report time and observation time (Part III).

# Appendix A: Typical LLM errors

From the first edition, all seen again:

- subclass confused with part-of or instance-of;
- duplicate concepts under different names;
- `rdfs:domain` / `rdfs:range` used as constraints (they are inference rules).

New in this edition, each seen in the example:

- **Meaning assumed from a field name.** The timestamp was modelled as the time
  of the incident; the publisher's help says it is the time of report.
- **The source's packaging taken for a concept.** Monthly download files
  modelled as a domain class.
- **Reuse by name.** A vocabulary term proposed because its name fits, while
  its definition does not (`hasCentroid`).
- **OWL 2 datatype map violations.** `xsd:gYearMonth` and `xsd:date` are not in
  the OWL 2 datatype map; a DL reasoner rejects them.
- **SHACL severity scope.** `sh:severity` on a node shape is not inherited by
  its property shapes; a warning shape must set it on each.
- **Silent tooling failures.** A SPARQL engine mishandled escaped prefixed
  names (`krimc:type\/18`) and returned an empty result without error. Two
  query layers caught it.
- **Host-language collisions.** In rdflib a namespace is a string, so
  `KDB.index` returned Python's `str.index` method instead of the IRI, and a
  mapping hint silently had no effect. Use `KDB["index"]`.
- **Correct but slow generated code.** A schema with no index on a foreign key.
- **Checklists that grow.** A first draft of concept statements with 21 entries
  where seven were needed.
- **Leaking the answer.** A validator that printed the computed answer to an
  expert who had not finished theirs.

Two errors were the human's, and the method should expect them: arithmetic
slips in hand answers, and a format rule (a mandatory separator) forgotten.
Neither side is the oracle.

# Appendix B: What changed from the first edition

| First edition | Second edition |
|---|---|
| Sequence starts with competency questions | Starts with reconnaissance and concept sentences; the warning about packaging |
| Competency questions become SPARQL tests | Expected answers by the expert, values hidden on failure, SPARQL and SQL must agree |
| Reuse before inventing | Reuse by definition, read the vocabulary's file; link fragile IDs; exact vs close match |
| Reasoner, report, CQ tests | Eight-section loop with negative tests, drift checks, concept tracing, loader tests |
| Excel glossary | Format by the reader's task: PDF glossary, Excel dictionary review, CSV samples |
| Shapes map onto the data model | The same, plus local definitions for reused properties and indexes by rule |
| Reference data with the ontology | Codelists with the ontology; large reference datasets in the database only |
| Lifecycle rules | The same, exercised: iterating on a release, deprecation in every artifact, pre-1.0 versions |

: The proof of concept {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

**References.** The day-to-day release practice (branches, CI checks, release
candidates, deprecation instead of deletion) follows the OBO Foundry and its
Ontology Development Kit. Competency questions come from eXtreme Design and
NeOn. Terminology: ISO 704 and ISO 1087; metadata registries: ISO/IEC 11179;
rules as sentences: SBVR and ORM; data governance: DAMA-DMBOK. Vocabularies
reused in the example: SKOS, Dublin Core, PROV-O, W3C WGS84, OGC GeoSPARQL, the
Czech semantic government vocabulary, and the ČSÚ codelist of municipalities.
